title: Steering
intro: The collision from Collide, at the speed where bouncing and passing are equally likely. Afterwards particle 2 (down the square) is on the upper side (x₂ < 20, the green band) only if the pair passed through each other. You cannot touch particle 2. You can only switch on an absorber on particle 1: key 1 swallows particle 1 wherever it is left of the middle (x₁ < 20, a vertical band), key 2 wherever it is right of it. A swallowed run does not count: the score is P_T among the runs where particle 1 survived.
goal: Make particle 2 end up in the green band (x₂ < 20) among the runs that count, by switching an absorber on particle 1 (key 1: left, key 2: right) at the right moment. The world observes at t = 11.

physics.point: Throwing away the runs where particle 1 is on one side leaves particle 2 almost surely on the other: that is steering. But the absolute chance of finding particle 2 in the band hardly moves. What you did to particle 1 only shows once the runs are sorted by particle 1's fate.
physics.eq: P(2 in band | 1 survived) ≈ 96 %,   P(2 in band) ≈ 50 % either way

idea: In 1935 Einstein, Podolsky and Rosen pointed out that for an entangled pair a measurement on one particle seems to decide the state of the other, however far away. Schrödinger, replying, called this steering, and found it deeply troubling. It is real: a choice made at particle 1 sorts particle 2 into one state or another.

After the collision the pair is r|bounced⟩ + t|passed⟩. If the pair passed through each other, particle 1 is on the right and particle 2 on the upper side; if it bounced, the other way round. The absorber on particle 1 is a detector that removes every run in which it found particle 1 on its side. Swallow particle 1 on the left, and every surviving run is a "passed" run: particle 2 is in the band.

Yet nothing reached particle 2. Its own statistics, counted over all runs, are the same with or without the absorber (the absorber acts on x₁ only, and for a pair that no longer interacts nothing done to x₁ changes the distribution of x₂). The effect lives entirely in the sorting, and sorting needs to know what happened to particle 1, information that can travel no faster than light. This is the no-signalling theorem, and why entanglement cannot send messages.

Timing matters: switch on before the collision has finished and you swallow the "passed" runs as well (and before t ≈ 5 nearly everything, which is scored as a loss); switch on too late and the absorber has not finished its job when the world observes.
maths: Long after the collision ψ ≈ r φ_L(x₁) φ_R(x₂) + t φ_R(x₁) φ_L(x₂). Particle 2's distribution on its own is the partial trace over particle 1:

Any operation on particle 1 alone, including a measurement or an absorber, satisfies Σₖ Mₖ†Mₖ = 1 summed over its outcomes ("absorbed" is one of them), so it leaves ρ₂ unchanged. Conditioned on the outcome "particle 1 survived the left absorber", the state is φ_R(x₁) φ_L(x₂): particle 2 is steered into φ_L.
Measured at t = 11 (score among survivors; P(2 in band) over all runs; surviving share):

maths.eq:
absorber          score   P(2 in band)  survived
none               53%        52%         100%
left, on at t = 4  53%*       13%          14%
left, on at t = 6  94%        34%          36%
left, on at t = 9  96%        49%          51%
left, on at t = 10 95%        50%          53%
right, on at t = 8  5%         2%          41%

maths: * below the post-selection floor of 25%: a run of survivors that small is not trusted.
try: Watch without touching anything: two blobs, and the band catches half.
Switch the left absorber on at the start: it swallows the whole pair.
Wait until the two blobs are clearly apart (about t = 9), then key 1: the upper-left blob fades and what is left is all in the band.
